answer: Pranam! I am AcharyaGPT. Ask me about Ayurvedic concepts such as Vata, Pitta and Kapha, or about a condition such as Amlapitta or Eka Kushtha, and I will explain what the Ayurvedic texts say.

Ayurveda is the traditional system of medicine that originated in India more than 3,000 years ago. The name comes from the Sanskrit words 'ayus' (life) and 'veda' (knowledge), so it means 'the knowledge of life'. Its two aims are to preserve the health of the healthy and to treat disease by restoring balance between the body, mind and environment.

Prabhava is the special or unique action of a substance that cannot be explained by its taste (rasa), potency (virya) or post-digestive effect (vipaka). It explains why two substances with similar properties can act differently.

I am AcharyaGPT, an educational assistant fine-tuned on Ayurvedic knowledge. I can explain Ayurvedic concepts such as Vata, Pitta and Kapha, their doshas and how they affect the body. I am not a substitute for a qualified doctor or Ayurvedic practitioner.
Jatharagni is the agni that digests the seven dhatus. It is nourished by all the dhatus, which means that imbalances in any dhatu will affect it. Its dosha is Pitta.
Vamana is therapeutic emesis (controlled, induced vomiting), one of the panchakarma therapies. It is mainly used to eliminate excess Kapha, for example in some respiratory and skin conditions.

Ojas is the refined essence of all seven dhatus. It is responsible for strength, vitality and immunity (vyadhikshamatva). When ojas is strong a person resists disease well; when it is depleted, immunity and vitality decline.
Virechana is therapeutic purgation, one of the panchakarma therapies. It is mainly used to eliminate excess Pitta from the body, for example in some skin diseases and digestive disorders.

Rasayana is the branch of Ayurveda devoted to rejuvenation. Rasayana herbs are used to promote longevity, strength, immunity, memory and overall vitality. Classic Ayurvedic rasayanas include Ashwagandha, Shatavari, Guduchi and Amalaki.

Vata is the dosha made of the elements space (akasha) and air (vayu). It governs all movement in the body, including breathing, circulation, nerve impulses, speech and elimination. Its qualities are dry, light, cold, rough, subtle and mobile.

Ghee (clarified butter, ghrita) is valued in Ayurveda for nourishing the tissues, kindling agni without aggravating Pitta, and acting as a carrier that takes herbs into the tissues. Many classical medicines are medicated ghees, such as Maha Tiktaka Ghrita.

Kapha is the dosha made of the elements earth (prithvi) and water (jala). It gives the body structure, stability, lubrication and strength, and it supports immunity. Its qualities are heavy, slow, cool, oily, smooth and stable.

Pitta is the dosha made of the elements fire (agni or tejas) and water (jala). It governs transformation in the body, such as digestion, metabolism, body temperature, vision and intellect. Its qualities are hot, sharp, light, slightly oily and liquid.
Medhya rasayana are Ayurvedic tonics for the mind that support memory, learning and calmness. They are nourishing, long-term herbs rather than quick fixes.
The main symptoms of Ama are sticky coating on tongue, sluggish digestion, heaviness and bad taste.

Raktamokshana is therapeutic bloodletting, described especially by Sushruta as a purification therapy. It is used for disorders of blood and Pitta, such as some skin diseases, and its methods include leech therapy (jalaukavacharana).
Common symptoms of Polio include muscle weakness, paralysis, fever and headache.
Malas are the waste products of the body. The three main malas are purisha (faeces), mutra (urine) and sweda (sweat). Their proper formation and elimination is necessary for good health.

The seven dhatus (body tissues) are Rasa (plasma), Rakta (blood), Mamsa (muscle), Meda (fat), Asthi (bone), Majja (marrow and nerve tissue) and Shukra (reproductive tissue). Each tissue is nourished in sequence from the one before it.
Common symptoms of Stroke include sudden numbness, weakness, confusion and difficulty speaking.
Neem pacifies Pitta.
The seven main srotas (channels) of the body are Pranavaha (breath), Udakavaha (water), Annavaha (food), Rasavaha, Raktavaha, Mamsavaha and Shukravaha.
Common symptoms of Malaria include fever, chills, headache, nausea and sweating.

Kubja is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Kyphosis in modern medicine. It mainly affects the musculoskeletal system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are hunched back, rounded upper spine, back pain and reduced height. Kubja is considered difficult to cure.

Palita is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Premature greying in modern medicine. It mainly affects the skin and the hair. It is predominantly a Pitta disorder. Its main symptoms are hair turns white or grey prematurely, may affect beard and eyebrows too and no other hair disorder. The prognosis of Palita is moderate.
Common symptoms of Vitiligo include loss of skin pigment and white patches on skin.

Samprapti is the pathogenesis stage: the way a dosha imbalance spreads through the body, the route it takes and the tissues it affects. It explains how the initial disturbance moves through the body, the channels it uses and the order of involvement.

Panchakarma is Ayurveda's set of five purification (shodhana) therapies - Vamana (therapeutic emesis), Virechana (therapeutic purgation), Basti (medicated enema), Nasya (nasal administration of medicine) and Raktamokshana (bloodletting). It is preceded by preparatory procedures (purvakarma) such as snehana (oleation) and svedana (sudation), and it should only be done under qualified supervision.

Adhman is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Tympanitis / Flatulence in modern medicine. It mainly affects the gastrointestinal (digestive) system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are abdominal bloating and distension, loud bowel sounds and passing of flatus relieves discomfort. Adhman is generally considered curable.
In Hindi, Stress is called तनाव. In Marathi it is called तणाव.

Sataru is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Erythroderma patches in modern medicine. It mainly affects the skin. It is predominantly a Pitta disorder. Its main symptoms are red patchy skin eruptions and may become generalised. The prognosis of Sataru is moderate.

Virya is the potency of a substance, its active heating or cooling energy. Ushna (heating) virya is found in foods and herbs that warm the body, such as ginger and chilies. Sheeta (cooling) virya is found in foods and herbs that cool the body, such as cucumbers and mint.

There are nine prakritis, made by combining the three doshas in different proportions. Vata (space and movement) is predominant in the head, chest and abdomen; Pitta (fire and transformation) in the eyes, skin, mouth and sweat glands; and Kapha (earth and water) in the eyes, ears, nose, mouth and skin.
Tulsi is predominantly a Vata disorder.
Common symptoms of Amebiasis include abdominal pain, diarrhea and fever.
In Hindi, Marburg is called मारबर्ग.

Murcha is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Syncope / Fainting in modern medicine. It mainly affects the nervous system. It is mainly caused by Vata and Pitta. Its main symptoms are sudden brief loss of consciousness, pallor and diaphoresis before faint and recovery within minutes. The prognosis of Murcha is variable and depends on the individual case.

Ksvathu is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Allergic rhinitis / Vasomotor rhinorrhoea in modern medicine. It mainly affects the nose. It is mainly caused by Vata and Kapha. Its main symptoms are paroxysmal sneezing, watery nasal discharge and nasal itching and congestion. The prognosis of Ksvathu is moderate.

Kacchu is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Prurigo / Skin itch (minor) in modern medicine. It mainly affects the skin. It is predominantly a Kapha disorder. Its main symptoms are itching without major skin lesion, scratching and excoriation marks. Kacchu is generally considered curable.

Sidhma is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Lichen planus / Pityriasis in modern medicine. It mainly affects the skin. It is mainly caused by Kapha and Vata. Its main symptoms are flat-topped purplish papules, wickham's striae on close inspection and itching and oral involvement. The prognosis of Sidhma is moderate.

Visvaci is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Brachial neuralgia in modern medicine. It mainly affects the nervous system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are pain from shoulder to arm and fingers, tingling and numbness in hand and worse with neck movement. The prognosis of Visvaci is moderate.
Common symptoms of Cystinosis include weakness, kidney issues and vision problems.

The three doshas are Vata, Pitta and Kapha. They are the functional principles that govern all activities of the body and mind. Health is a state in which the three doshas are in balance, and disease arises when one or more of them become imbalanced.
In Hindi, Cold is called सर्दी.

Udavarta is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Reverse peristalsis / Suppression disorders in modern medicine. It mainly affects the gastrointestinal (digestive) system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are upward movement of gases (belching, reflux), headache and chest discomfort and history of suppressing natural urges. The prognosis of Udavarta is moderate.

Nadi pariksha is Ayurvedic pulse examination, usually felt at the radial artery of the wrist. It is used to assess the state of the doshas; a Vata pulse is traditionally described as moving like a snake, a Pitta pulse like a frog and a Kapha pulse like a swan.

Kacchapa is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Adenoma of palate in modern medicine. It mainly affects the mouth. It is predominantly a Kapha disorder. Its main symptoms are hard swelling on palate resembling tortoise back, slow growing and difficulty in speech. The prognosis of Kacchapa is moderate.
In Hindi, Pneumonia is called न्यूमोनिया.

Carmadala is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Erythromelalgia in modern medicine. It mainly affects the skin and the nails. It is mainly caused by Vata and Kapha. Its main symptoms are red, irritated skin around nail, swelling and burning. Carmadala is generally considered curable.

Netranadi is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Chronic dacrocystitis / Epiphora in modern medicine. It mainly affects the eyes. It is predominantly a Kapha disorder. Its main symptoms are chronic watering of eye, swelling at inner corner of eye and mucopurulent discharge on pressure over lacrimal sac. The prognosis of Netranadi is moderate.

Vasameha is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Lipuria in modern medicine. It mainly affects the urinary system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are fatty or oily appearance to urine and difficult to treat. Vasameha is considered difficult to cure.
The main symptoms of Pangu are paralysis of both legs, loss of sensation below lesion and bladder and bowel dysfunction.

Amlapitta is a condition described in the Madhava Nidana that corresponds to Hyperacidity / GERD in modern medicine. It mainly affects the gastrointestinal (digestive) system. It is predominantly a Pitta disorder. Its main symptoms are burning sensation in chest/throat (heartburn), sour belching and nausea worse after spicy food. Amlapitta is generally considered curable.

Galaganda is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Goitre (thyroid) in modern medicine. It mainly affects the thyroid gland. It is mainly caused by Kapha and Vata. Its main symptoms are swelling of thyroid, compression symptoms, hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. The prognosis of Galaganda is moderate.
Guduchi is considered a rasayana because it promotes longevity and overall health and immunity.
Yoga and physical therapy suggested for Cold include Restorative Yoga and Breathing.

Mutraksaya is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Suppression of urine in modern medicine. It mainly affects the urinary system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are complete absence of urine output (anuria), renal failure features and oedema. Mutraksaya is considered difficult to cure.

Mamsatana is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Cellulitis / Cancer of throat in modern medicine. It mainly affects the throat. Its predominant factors are Pitta and Rakta (blood). Its main symptoms are spreading red or indurated throat swelling, deep throat pain and dysphagia. Mamsatana is considered difficult to cure.
In Ayurveda, Spongy corresponds to Sitada.

Anilaroha is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Upward movement of Vata in modern medicine. It mainly affects the gastrointestinal (digestive) system and the whole body (it is a systemic condition). It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are upward-moving gas, belching, chest tightness and bloating. The prognosis of Anilaroha is moderate.

Galasundi is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Uvulitis / Elongated uvula in modern medicine. It mainly affects the throat. It is predominantly a Kapha disorder. Its main symptoms are elongated uvula, throat discomfort, gagging and choking sensation. Galasundi is generally considered curable.
In Hindi, Depression is called अवसाद. In Marathi it is called उदासीनता.

Adhimantha is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Glaucoma in modern medicine. It mainly affects the eyes. It is mainly caused by Vata and Pitta. Its main symptoms are severe eye pain, headache (temporal region), halos around lights, reduced peripheral vision and nausea (acute cases). The prognosis of Adhimantha is moderate.

Galasaluka is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Adenoids in modern medicine. It mainly affects the throat. It is predominantly a Kapha disorder. Its main symptoms are mouth breathing, snoring, nasal obstruction, recurrent infections and hyponasal voice. The prognosis of Galasaluka is moderate.

Balakshaya is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Loss of strength / Asthenia in modern medicine. It is a systemic condition that affects the whole body. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are generalised weakness, reduced physical performance and easy fatigability. The prognosis of Balakshaya is moderate.
In Hindi, Joint Pain is called जोड़ दर्द. In Marathi it is called सांधेदुखी.

Ayurveda describes six tastes (shad rasa) - Madhura (sweet), Amla (sour), Lavana (salty), Katu (pungent), Tikta (bitter) and Kashaya (astringent). Sweet, sour and salty pacify Vata; sweet, bitter and astringent pacify Pitta; and pungent, bitter and astringent pacify Kapha.

Kloma Roga is a condition described in the Ashtanga Hridayam that corresponds to Pancreatic diseases in modern medicine. It mainly affects the gastrointestinal (digestive) system and the pancreas. It is mainly caused by Pitta and Vata. Its main symptoms are epigastric pain radiating to back, fatty stool (steatorrhoea) and weight loss and glucose intolerance. Kloma Roga is considered difficult to cure.
Common symptoms of Dengue Fever include high fever, joint pain and skin rash.

Rasa is the taste of a substance, such as sweet, sour, salty, bitter, astringent and oily. Vipaka is the post-digestive effect of a substance, the taste-like effect that appears after digestion is complete. There are three vipakas - madhura (sweet), amla (sour) and katu (pungent).

Bhagandara is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Fistula-in-ano in modern medicine. It mainly affects the anorectal region. It is a tridoshic disorder involving all three doshas - Vata, Pitta and Kapha. Its main symptoms are external opening near anus, discharge of pus or faeces and recurrent perianal abscess. The prognosis of Bhagandara is moderate.

Vilambika is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Food poisoning / Ileus in modern medicine. It mainly affects the gastrointestinal (digestive) system. It is mainly caused by Vata and Kapha. Its main symptoms are slow onset nausea, abdominal pain, delayed vomiting (4–8 hours after eating) and heaviness and distension. The prognosis of Vilambika is moderate.
In Hindi, Stroke is called स्ट्रोक.

Sukrameha is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Glycosuria (alimentary) in modern medicine. It mainly affects the urinary system. It is predominantly a Kapha disorder. Its main symptoms are sweet, cane-juice like urine and excessive urination after meals. The prognosis of Sukrameha is moderate.

Vata Shotha is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Oedema (Vata) in modern medicine. It mainly affects the cardiovascular system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are pitting oedema that is dry and painful and associated with joint pain and dryness. The prognosis of Vata Shotha is moderate.

Vatakantaka is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Ankle sprain / Plantar fasciitis in modern medicine. It mainly affects the musculoskeletal system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are heel pain on first steps in morning, tenderness at heel or ankle and aggravated by prolonged standing. Vatakantaka is generally considered curable.

In Ayurveda, Polio is associated with an imbalance of Vata and Pitta, and people with a Vata constitution are considered more prone to it. Common symptoms include muscle weakness, paralysis, fever and headache.

Bandhyathva is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Infertility / Sterility in modern medicine. It mainly affects the female reproductive system (it is a gynaecological condition). It is mainly caused by Vata and Kapha. Its main symptoms are inability to conceive, ovulatory dysfunction and uterine abnormality. The prognosis of Bandhyathva is moderate.

Sarpa Visha is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Snake / Scorpion sting in modern medicine. It is a systemic condition that affects the whole body. It is classified as Agantuja: it is caused by external factors such as injury, poison or bites rather than primarily by a dosha imbalance. Its main symptoms are bite or sting history, local swelling, pain and systemic toxicity. The prognosis of Sarpa Visha is moderate.

Svarabheda is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Hoarseness of voice in modern medicine. It mainly affects the throat. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are change in voice quality (rough or breathy), vocal fatigue and possible complete aphonia. The prognosis of Svarabheda is variable and depends on the individual case.

Tamra Kotha is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Green gangrene in modern medicine. It mainly affects the body in a way that needs surgical care (it is a surgical condition). Its predominant factors are Pitta and Rakta (blood). Its main symptoms are tissue necrosis with greenish discolouration, foul smell, severe pain and systemic toxicity. Tamra Kotha is considered difficult to cure.
Nasya is used for conditions such as colds, headaches and respiratory issues.

The panchamahabhutas (five great elements) are Akasha (space or ether), Vayu (air), Agni or Tejas (fire), Jala or Apas (water) and Prithvi (earth). Everything in nature, including the body, is made of them; Vata comes from space and air, Pitta from fire and water, and Kapha from earth and water.

The three great classics (Brihat Trayi) are the Charaka Samhita (internal medicine), the Sushruta Samhita (surgery) and the Ashtanga Hridaya of Vagbhata. The three lesser classics (Laghu Trayi) are the Madhava Nidana (diagnosis), the Sharangadhara Samhita (pharmacy and formulations) and the Bhavaprakasha (materia medica).

Vrkka Sula is a condition described in the Ashtanga Hridayam that corresponds to Renal colic in modern medicine. It mainly affects the urinary system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are sudden severe flank pain radiating to groin, restlessness (can't find comfortable position) and haematuria. Vrkka Sula is generally considered curable.

Gandha Roga is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Smell disorders in modern medicine. It mainly affects the nose. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are loss of smell, distorted perception of smell and nasal congestion. The prognosis of Gandha Roga is moderate.

Varna Hani is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Ocular pain / Trigeminal neuralgia in modern medicine. It mainly affects the eyes. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are visible protrusion from eye, severe pain, vision loss and photophobia. Varna Hani is considered difficult to cure.

In Ayurveda, Pinta is associated with an imbalance of Pitta, and people with a Pitta constitution are considered more prone to it. Common symptoms include skin lesions, joint pain and swelling. Herbs traditionally used include Neem and Turmeric.

Bija Dushti is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Reproductive fluid disorders in modern medicine. It mainly affects the reproductive system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are abnormal semen, reduced libido, subfertility and painful ejaculation. The prognosis of Bija Dushti is moderate.
In Hindi, Fibromyalgia is called फाइब्रोमाइल्जिया.

Padbhramsha is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Cracked heels / Rhagades in modern medicine. It mainly affects the skin. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are deep painful cracks in heel skin, bleeding from fissures, dry and thickened skin. Padbhramsha is generally considered curable.

Vataja Mada is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Vata intoxication in modern medicine. It mainly affects the nervous system and the mind (it is a mental disorder). It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are agitation and delirium and tremors and fearfulness. Vataja Mada is generally considered curable.

Sattva, Rajas and Tamas are the three qualities (gunas) of the mind. Sattva stands for clarity, balance and purity; Rajas for activity and restlessness; and Tamas for inertia and dullness. Rajas and Tamas are called the manas doshas because their excess disturbs the mind.

Dhatu Ksaya is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Tissue depletion disorders in modern medicine. It is a systemic condition that affects the whole body. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are wasting of specific dhatu, weakness, pallor and reduced endurance. Dhatu Ksaya is considered difficult to cure.
In Hindi, Brain Tumors is called मस्तिष्क ट्यूमर. In Marathi it is called मेंदूचा गाठ.

Danta Chalu is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Loose tooth in modern medicine. It mainly affects the teeth. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are tooth mobility, gum recession and pain on chewing. The prognosis of Danta Chalu is moderate.

Jihvastambha is a condition described in the Madhava Nidana that corresponds to Paralysis of tongue in modern medicine. It mainly affects the mouth. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are inability to move tongue, difficulty speaking (dysarthria) and difficulty chewing and swallowing. Jihvastambha is considered difficult to cure.
In Ayurveda, Scrofula corresponds to Gandamala.

Sarvangavata is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Quadriplegia / Poly-neuropathy in modern medicine. It mainly affects the nervous system. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are weakness or paralysis of all four limbs, loss of sensation and bladder/bowel dysfunction. Sarvangavata is considered difficult to cure.

Manyastambha is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Cervical spondylosis in modern medicine. It mainly affects the musculoskeletal system and the nervous system. It is mainly caused by Vata and Kapha. Its main symptoms are neck stiffness, difficulty rotating head, pain and muscle spasm. The prognosis of Manyastambha is moderate.
In Ayurveda, Vomiting corresponds to Chardi.
In Hindi, Insomnia is called अनिद्रा.
The main symptoms of Nasarsas are soft, grape-like growths in nasal cavity, bilateral nasal obstruction and loss of smell.
In Hindi, Bell's Palsy is called बेल्स पाल्सी. In Marathi it is called बेल्स पॅल्सी.

Garbha Roga is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Pregnancy-related diseases in modern medicine. It mainly affects the female reproductive system (it is a gynaecological condition). It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are vaginal bleeding, pain, swelling, halos around cervix and photophobia. The prognosis of Garbha Roga is variable and depends on the individual case.
Common symptoms of Cerebral Palsy include muscle weakness, spasticity and difficulty with movement.

Kama (Lust) is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Desire / Lust in modern medicine. It is a mental disorder: it affects the mind. It is predominantly a Kapha disorder. Its main symptoms are excessive sexual desire, difficulty concentrating, insomnia and anxiety. The prognosis of Kama (Lust) is moderate.
In Hindi, Buruli Ulcer is called बुरुली अल्सर.
In Hindi, Yellow Fever is called पीला बुखार. In Marathi it is called पिवळा ताप.

Vata Trshna is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Vata thirst disorder in modern medicine. It is a systemic condition that affects the whole body. It is predominantly a Vata disorder. Its main symptoms are thirst with dry throat, hoarseness, restlessness and variable intensity. Vata Trshna is generally considered curable.

Vikriti is the current state of the doshas in a person, which can differ from their natural constitution (prakriti). A gap between vikriti and prakriti indicates imbalance, and Ayurvedic care aims to bring vikriti back towards prakriti.
In Ayurveda, Pricking corresponds to Vata Rogi - Toda.

In Ayurveda, Anemia is associated with an imbalance of Pitta, and people with a Pitta constitution are considered more prone to it. Common symptoms include fatigue, pale skin and shortness of breath. Herbs traditionally used include Iron-Rich Foods (Spinach, Red Meat). Helpful yoga includes Iron Supplements and Regular Monitoring.
The main symptoms of Pravahika are mucoid bloody stools, tenesmus, colicky pain and fever.
In Ayurveda, Jaundiced corresponds to Nanatmaja Pitta 8 - Haritanetrata.

Krtrima Visha is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Artificial / Prepared poison in modern medicine. It is a systemic condition that affects the whole body. It is classified as Agantuja: it is caused by external factors such as injury, poison or bites rather than primarily by a dosha imbalance. Its main symptoms are intentional poisoning symptoms, multi-organ effects and sudden onset. Krtrima Visha is considered difficult to cure.

Hemanta Jwara is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Winter fever in modern medicine. It is a systemic condition that affects the whole body. It is predominantly a Kapha disorder. Its main symptoms are winter fever, chills, Kapha-Vata predominance and nasal congestion. Hemanta Jwara is generally considered curable.
The main symptoms of Carmadala are red, irritated skin in folds or contact areas, scaling or weeping and worse with moisture.
In Ayurveda, Papilloma corresponds to Padma Kantaka.
In Hindi, Menopause is called रजोनिवृत्ति.

Drishti Roga is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Vision disorders in modern medicine. It mainly affects the eyes. It is mainly caused by Vata and Pitta. Its main symptoms are blurred vision, reduced acuity, double vision and night blindness. The prognosis of Drishti Roga is variable and depends on the individual case.
The main symptoms of Yoni Daha are burning sensation in vaginal area, redness and discharge and pain during intercourse.

Mutragranthi is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Prostatic tumour / Bladder tumour in modern medicine. It mainly affects the urinary system. Its predominant factors are Kapha and Meda (fat tissue). Its main symptoms are difficulty initiating urination, weak stream, haematuria and post-void dribbling. Mutragranthi is considered difficult to cure.
The main symptoms of Tilkalaka are small, flat, pigmented spots, non-elevated and no symptoms.
In Ayurveda, Twitching corresponds to Vata Rogi - Spandana.

Kaphaja Jvara is a condition described in the Charaka Samhita that corresponds to Mild continuous fever with heaviness in modern medicine. It is a systemic condition that affects the whole body. It is predominantly a Kapha disorder. Its main symptoms are low-grade persistent fever, heaviness, drowsiness, white coating on tongue and loss of taste and appetite. Kaphaja Jvara is generally considered curable.

Arsha (Bahya) is a condition described in the Madhava Nidana that corresponds to External haemorrhoids in modern medicine. It mainly affects the anorectal region. It is mainly caused by Vata and Pitta. Its main symptoms are external piles, pain, pruritus ani, bleeding and prolapse. Arsha (Bahya) is generally considered curable.

Charma Kupita is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Dermatitis contact in modern medicine. It mainly affects the skin. Its predominant factors are Pitta and external causes (Agantuja). Its main symptoms are redness, itching, blistering after skin contact with irritant and burning. Charma Kupita is generally considered curable.
Ashwagandha is an adaptogen that helps the body manage stress. It is mainly used to support strength, stamina, sleep and resilience to stress.

Vinata Pidika is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Discoloured diabetic swelling in modern medicine. It mainly affects metabolism. It is predominantly a Pitta disorder. Its main symptoms are discoloured (bluish-red) swelling on diabetic skin and slow healing. The prognosis of Vinata Pidika is moderate.

Dagdha Vrana is a condition described in the Sushruta Samhita that corresponds to Burn wound in modern medicine. It mainly affects the skin. Its predominant factors are Pitta and external causes (Agantuja). Its main symptoms are wound from thermal injury, redness, blisters, or charring by degree, severe pain (first/second degree) and no pain (third degree). Dagdha Vrana is generally considered curable.
The main symptoms of Karnanada are severe ear pain, swelling and redness of pinna and hearing loss.

In Ayurveda, Tetanus is associated with an imbalance of Vata and Kapha, and people with a Vata-Kapha constitution are considered more prone to it. Common symptoms include muscle stiffness, spasms and difficulty swallowing.
In Hindi, Lowe Syndrome is called लोवे सिंड्रोम.

In Ayurveda, Lupus is associated with an imbalance of Pitta and Vata, and people with a Pitta-Vata constitution are considered more prone to it. Common symptoms include fatigue, joint pain, skin rashes and photosensitivity. Herbs traditionally used include Ashwagandha and Turmeric. Helpful yoga includes Stress Management and Regular Exercise.

Trikatu means 'three pungents'. It is a classical Ayurvedic combination of Shunthi (dry ginger), Maricha (black pepper) and Pippali (long pepper), traditionally used to kindle agni and reduce Kapha and ama.

Shodhana (purification) therapy is the main treatment of Ayurveda; it is only after adequate purification that the body can accept new Agni (digestive fire) and Dhatu (tissue). Palliative or shamana treatment is a branch of Ayurveda that deals with the soul of the body - the jiva. It is the soul that feels pain, hunger, thirst and other sensations, and it is the soul that is pleased or distressed by treatment. Ayurveda is an ancient system of medicine originating from India, which emphasizes the balance of mind, body, and spirit to achieve optimal health and well-being. It is based on the principles of three fundamental energies or doshas—Vata, Pitta, and Kapha—that govern physiological and psychological functions. Ayurveda incorporates lifestyle, diet, herbal medicine, yoga, and detoxification practices to maintain harmony within the individual and with nature.

**Prabhava** is a concept in Ayurveda referring to the unique and specific therapeutic action of a drug or substance that cannot be explained by its **Rasa** (taste), **Guna** (qualities), **Virya** (potency), or **Vipaka** (post-digestive effect). It is the inherent, irreplaceable power of a drug that contributes to its efficacy and is distinct from its general properties. Prabhava is considered a qualitative property that enhances the pharmacological action of a substance.

Jatharagni is the digestive fire in Ayurveda, responsible for digesting food and converting it into energy. A balanced Jatharagni ensures proper digestion and overall health, while an imbalance can lead to digestive disorders and other health issues.

Vata dosha is one of the three fundamental energies (doshas) in Ayurveda, representing air and space. It governs all movement in the body, including circulation, nerve function, and elimination. Vata is associated with qualities like lightness, dryness, and mobility. When balanced, Vata promotes creativity, flexibility, and mental clarity. However, an excess of Vata can lead to issues such as anxiety, insomnia, constipation, and joint pain. It is best balanced through routine, warm foods, and grounding practices.

When balanced, Kapha promotes vitality, endurance, and a sense of security. However, when imbalanced, it can lead to conditions such as congestion, weight gain, and sluggishness. Kapha is most active during the early morning and is associated with the earth element.

Pitta dosha is one of the three fundamental energies (doshas) in Ayurveda, representing the fire and water elements. It governs all metabolic processes, digestion, and transformation in the body. Pitta is associated with heat, metabolism, and intelligence. It regulates body temperature, digestion (agni), and the balance of bodily fluids. Pitta individuals are typically of medium build, have a warm body temperature, and are often sharp-minded and passionate. Imbalances in Pitta can lead to issues such as inflammation, acidity, and irritability.

The quality and quantity of **mala** reflect the state of **agni** and **dosha** (body constitution). Healthy **mala** is firm, well-formed, and easily expelled, while impaired **mala** can indicate **agni** imbalance or **ama** (toxins) accumulation.

Proper elimination of **mala** is essential for maintaining **sama dosha**, **sama agni**, and overall **health**. Ayurveda emphasizes **snehana** (oleation) and **swedana** (sudation) to facilitate the smooth passage of **mala** and prevent **ama** buildup.

The six rasas (tastes) in Ayurveda are the fundamental tastes that are derived from food and are essential for nourishment and health. They are:

1. **Madhura (Sweet)**: Found in fruits, honey, and sugar. It nourishes, strengthens, and balances Vata and Kapha.
2. **Amla (Sour)**: Found in citrus fruits and fermented foods. It stimulates digestion, enhances appetite, and balances Vata.
3. **Lavana (Salty)**: Found in sea salt and certain vegetables. It aids digestion, regulates body fluids, and balances Kapha.
4. **Tikta (Bitter)**: Found in leafy greens and some herbs. It detoxifies, reduces Kapha, and promotes longevity.
5. **Katu (Pungent)**: Found in spices like ginger and black pepper. It enhances digestion, sharpens the mind, and balances Kapha.
6. **Kashaya (Astringent)**: Found in legumes and certain fruits. It tones tissues, reduces excess Kapha, and promotes healing.

Each rasa has specific effects on the doshas and the body, and a balanced intake is essential for maintaining health.

In Ayurveda, **Rasa** and **Vipaka** are two distinct properties of food and herbs, related to their effects on the body.

- **Rasa** refers to the **taste** (or flavor) of a substance, such as sweet, sour, salty, etc. It is the initial effect of the food on the palate and is responsible for the immediate sensation.

- **Vipaka** refers to the **final effect** or **post-digestive effect** of a substance after digestion. It is the residual effect that remains after the rasa and digested nutrients are absorbed. Vipaka is determined by the dominant taste of the food after digestion.

For example:
- A **sweet**-tasting food (like sugar) has a **sweet** rasa and a **sweet** vipaka.
- A **sour**-tasting food (like lemon) has a **sour** rasa and a **pungent** vipaka.

Understanding both rasa and vipaka helps in determining the overall effect of food on the doshas and the body.

Svarabheda, in Ayurveda, refers to the differentiation of the three fundamental sounds or vibrations—**Sva**, **Bheda**, and **Svar**—that are considered the basis of all creation. These sounds are believed to originate from the primordial sound **Om** and are associated with the three doshas (Vata, Pitta, Kapha) and the three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas).

- **Sva** represents the essence or self, associated with **Sattva** guna and **Kapha** dosha.
- **Bheda** signifies differentiation or change, linked to **Rajas** guna and **Pitta** dosha.
- **Svar** denotes vibration or sound, connected to **Tamas** guna and **Vata** dosha.

Svarabheda is a concept used in Ayurveda to understand the fundamental nature of existence and the interplay of the doshas and gunas in the universe and within the human body. It is also relevant in the context of mantra and meditation practices, where the sounds are used to balance the doshas and achieve harmony.

Tamra Kotha is a classical Ayurvedic text attributed to the sage Tamra, which is considered a significant work in the field of Ayurveda. The text is part of the "Shodhaka Khanda" (the branch dealing with the study of diseases) in Ayurvedic literature and is often studied alongside other foundational texts like the Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita. It provides insights into the principles of disease management, the use of herbs, and the importance of maintaining balance in the body's three doshas.

However, it is important to note that Tamra Kotha is not as widely referenced or studied as the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas, and its availability in modern times is limited. For a comprehensive understanding of Ayurveda, it is recommended to refer to the more well-known and extensively studied texts.

The **Panchamahabhuta theory** is a fundamental concept in Ayurveda, representing the five basic elements that constitute all matter in the universe and the human body. These elements are:

1. **Space (Akasha)**: Associated with sound and the sense of hearing. It provides the medium for sound waves and is linked to the ears.
2. **Air (Vayu)**: Associated with movement, circulation, and the sense of touch. It governs respiration, movement, and the nervous system.
3. **Fire (Tejas)**: Associated with heat, digestion, and the sense of sight. It governs metabolism, digestion, and transformation.
4. **Water (Jala)**: Associated with liquidity, cohesion, and the sense of taste. It is linked to bodily fluids, circulation, and nourishment.
5. **Earth (Prithvi)**: Associated with solidity, structure, and the sense of smell. It forms the physical structure of the body and provides stability.

In Ayurveda, these elements are not only the building blocks of the physical world but also the basis of the three doshas (Vata, Pitta, Kapha), which are the fundamental energies that govern physiological and psychological functions. Balance

Here are some of the important Ayurvedic texts:

1. **Charaka Samhita** - A foundational text on medicine, authored by Charaka, focusing on internal medicine, physiology, and pathology.

2. **Sushruta Samhita** - A major text on surgery, authored by Sushruta, covering surgical procedures, anatomy, and medical instruments.

3. **Ashtanga Hridaya** - A comprehensive text compiled by Sushruta's disciples, serving as a key reference for Ayurvedic practice.

4. **Ashtanga Sangraha** - A concise summary of the Ashtanga Hridaya, also authored by Vagbhata.

5. **Bhela Samhita** - A text focusing on the role of the physician and the importance of patient care.

6. **Sharangdhar Samhita** - A text that provides detailed information on Ayurvedic formulations and their uses.

7. **Dhanvantari Samhita** - A text that includes various aspects of Ayurveda, including diet, lifestyle, and disease management.

These texts form the core of Ayurvedic knowledge and are essential for understanding its principles and practices.

Cerebral Palsy (CP) is a group of neurological disorders that affect movement, muscle tone, and posture. Common symptoms include:

2. **Muscle stiffness (spasticity)**: Tight or stiff muscles, often in the legs or arms.
3. **Muscle weakness**: Reduced strength in one or more limbs.
4. **Uncontrolled movements**: Involuntary or repetitive movements.
5. **Delayed developmental milestones**: Such as sitting, crawling, or walking later than typical.
6. **Speech and language difficulties**: Slurred speech or trouble with communication.
7. **Epilepsy**: Seizures may occur in some individuals.
8. **Sensory issues**: Problems with vision, hearing, or touch.
9. **Learning disabilities**: Some individuals may have intellectual disabilities.
10. **Swallowing difficulties (dysphagia)**: Can lead to feeding challenges.

These symptoms vary widely depending on the type and severity of CP.

In **Kama Sutra**, Kama is celebrated as a legitimate aspect of human experience, but in **Ayurvedic philosophy**, it is balanced with **Dharma** and **Santosha** (contentment) to maintain harmony within the self and society.

Bhasmaka, also known as *Bhasma* in Ayurveda, refers to a category of medicines prepared through a specific calcination process. The doshic involvement in Bhasmaka depends on the specific type of Bhasma, as different metals and minerals are used, each with their own inherent properties and effects on the doshas.

For example:

- **Shilajit Bhasma** is primarily associated with **Vata** and **Kapha** due to its heavy, unctuous nature.
- **Rajat Bhasma (Silver Bhasma)** is known to pacify **Vata** and **Kapha** and is often used for neurological and skin disorders.
- **Tamra Bhasma (Copper Bhasma)** is associated with **Pitta** and is used for conditions involving heat and inflammation.

In general, Bhasmas are considered to have a **heavy, unctuous, and cooling** effect, which tends to pacify **Vata** and **Pitta**, while potentially aggravating **Kapha** if not used in proper dosage. It is important to consult an Ayurvedic practitioner for individualized use.

For precise diagnosis and treatment, consultation with an Ayurvedic practitioner is recommended.

Atiyoga, also known as Virechana, is a therapeutic Ayurvedic procedure primarily used to eliminate toxins (Ama) from the body, particularly from the digestive tract. It is one of the Panchakarma therapies and is mainly indicated for Pitta dosha imbalance.

### Key Points:
- **Purpose**: To detoxify the body, especially the small intestine, and balance Pitta.
- **Method**: It involves the administration of a mild laxative (such as Triphala or Senna) to induce a controlled bowel movement.
- **Indications**: Pitta-related disorders like acidity, skin diseases, and digestive issues.
- **Contraindications**: Not recommended for individuals with weak digestion, constipation, or during pregnancy.

Virechana is typically performed under the guidance of an experienced Ayurvedic practitioner.

Ksayaja Svarabheda refers to the classification of doshas (Vata, Pitta, Kapha) based on their capacity to cause tissue breakdown (ksaya) or degeneration. It is a concept used in Ayurveda to understand how the doshas influence the body's tissues (dhatus) and their potential to lead to degenerative conditions.

There are three types of Ksayaja Svarabheda:

1. **Vata Ksayaja**: Vata dosha is primarily responsible for degeneration and breakdown of tissues. It is associated with dryness, lightness, and movement, which can lead to tissue wasting.

2. **Pitta Ksayaja**: Pitta dosha is linked to metabolic processes and can cause degeneration through excessive heat and digestion. It is associated with inflammation and tissue breakdown due to overactivity.

3. **Kapha Ksayaja**: Kapha dosha, while typically associated with structure and stability, can also contribute to degeneration when imbalanced. It may lead to congestion and slow degeneration of tissues.

Understanding Ksayaja Svarabheda helps in diagnosing and treating conditions related to tissue degeneration, as it indicates which dosha is primarily involved in the process.

Prana, Udana, Samana, Vyana, and Apana are the five Vayus (principles of motion) in Ayurveda, each governing specific physiological and psychological functions:

1. **Prana** – Governs inhalation, sensory functions, and the upper part of the body. It is responsible for life force, respiration, and mental alertness.

2. **Udana** – Associated with exhalation, speech, growth, and the upward movement of energy. It influences voice, expression, and the ability to rise or achieve goals.

3. **Samana** – Regulates digestion and assimilation in the abdomen. It balances the body's internal functions and maintains equilibrium.

4. **Vyana** – Governs circulation and movement throughout the body. It is responsible for distributing energy and maintaining bodily functions.

5. **Apana** – Controls elimination, including excretion, menstruation, and childbirth. It is associated with the lower part of the body and the downward movement of energy.

These Vayus work together to maintain the balance of life processes in the body.

3. **Intellectual disability** and developmental delays.
4. **Motor coordination issues**, including ataxia and gait abnormalities.
5. **Breathing irregularities**, such as apnea and hyperventilation.

5. **Small, Frequent Meals:** Eat smaller, more frequent meals to reduce the feeling of fullness, which can make breathing more difficult.

The doshic involvement in Vishada (Despair) is Tridosha (Vata, Pitta, and Kapha), although the condition is primarily associated with a predominance of all three doshas. According to Ayurveda, while any disease involves all three doshas, the manifestation and treatment focus on the dosha with the majority involvement. In the case of Vishada, the treatment principles emphasize balancing all three doshas.
The doshic involvement in Dipta is primarily Pitta.
The doshic involvement in Sanyasa is primarily Vata and Pitta.
The doshic involvement in Parikartika is primarily Vata and Pitta.
The doshic involvement in Karnanada is primarily Vata, with Kapha also being involved, though Vata predominates.

The doshic involvement in Bandhyathva is Tridosha (Vata, Pitta, and Kapha). However, the condition is primarily associated with an imbalance of all three doshas, with the predominance depending on individual constitution and specific symptoms.
The symptoms seen in Kama (Lust) include excessive sexual preoccupation, intrusive thoughts, and impulsive behaviour.
The symptoms seen in Padbhramsha are: inability to lift the forefoot, steppage gait, and peroneal nerve involvement.
The source for Sukrameha is the Charaka Samhita.
The symptoms seen in Carmadala include nail deformity, discoloration, or brittleness, pain around the nail fold, and possible discharge.
The symptoms seen in Sanyasa are total loss of consciousness, no response to external stimuli, and a severely reduced Glasgow Coma Scale.
The source for Padbhramsha is the Madhava Nidana.
The symptoms seen in Parikartika are: Sharp cutting pain during defaecation, Bright red blood on stool surface, and Pain persisting after defaecation.
The Ayurvedic classic that is the source for Carmadala is the **Sushruta Samhita**.
The symptoms seen in Karnanada are ringing, buzzing, or hissing in the ear, with no external source of sound. It may be unilateral or bilateral.
The source for Sanyasa is the **Charaka Samhita**.
The source for Parikartika is the Sushruta Samhita.
The source for Mahasausira is the Sushruta Samhita.
The symptoms seen in Bandhyathva include failure to conceive after one year of unprotected intercourse, which may be primary or secondary, and no specific symptoms are always present.
The source for Bandhyathva is the Charaka Samhita.
